method: Complete Chinese source reading and paragraph-aligned English restoration, followed after all five essays were saved by a complete paragraph-by-paragraph reread of the saved English against the Chinese source. Terminology and cross-essay checks incorporated the independent audit’s specific corrections. This record describes translator self-review, not an independent review.

review_scope.source: The complete title, deck, and body in sources/ep06.json through sources/ep10.json; the former English was used only to identify omissions and additions, not as the translation source.
review_scope.sequence: All five restorations were saved before the full batch reread. Corrections were then saved, the affected passages reread, and final metadata, paragraph, markup, source-hash, and language checks run.
focus: Examples and rhetorical pauses, including short standalone paragraphs.
Constitutive conditions versus good intentions; actual stopping positions versus speech.
Who establishes a person’s own law.
The four distinct grounds for return and each reason it cannot be adopted by SAE.
Expression and manipulation using the same emotional gate.
Qualifications, concessions to Plato, and counterquestions left unanswered by the Chinese source.

cross_article_findings: The abbreviated former English retained many main conclusions but merged concrete scenes and rhetorical turns and added section headings. The full versions preserve the source paragraph sequence without headings.

EP06 distinguishes the ruled person’s benefit as a constitutive condition from a stopping point held by the other party. EP07 likewise distinguishes the city’s assignment from the person’s establishment of their own law.
EP06, EP08, EP09, and EP10 formerly added explanatory answers or remedies not supplied by the Chinese. Those additions are absent; practical objections remain live rather than being resolved for SAE.
EP08 preserves the distinction between judging the shape of a move and condemning a storyteller. Useful or sincere stories can still be made into unquestionable foundations.
EP09 preserves all four grounds for return, their different dependencies, and the four different reasons SAE cannot take them over. Ordinary necessity is not labeled with the technical cannot-not.
EP10 preserves both the expression/manipulation mechanism and the question of the defender’s own susceptibility. No invented test is offered to settle it.
The source’s interpretive claims, including EP10’s three levels and EP07’s lifetime-watch challenge, have been translated as written rather than silently normalized or answered.
corrections: EP06 paragraph 2: made the repeated interruption attempts idiomatic without changing their number or meaning.
EP06 paragraph 18: changed payment to reward so the term does not prematurely narrow the following account to money.

EP06 paragraph 50: after the independent audit, replaced disposal with handling and explicitly named the fully stripped-down relation; the passage does not claim that the person is literally discarded.
EP07 deck and paragraph 14: clarified that the person establishes their own law and polished the phrase one’s own. Paragraph 31 now uses shortchanged rather than suffer for the statue’s eyes.
EP08 paragraph 32: removed the narrowing word motives; the source separates the move generally from good/bad evaluation.
EP09 paragraphs 21, 22, and 28: after the independent audit, replaced cannot-not/cannot not with must/necessity to avoid conflating Platonic compulsory return with SAE’s technical 14DD term.
EP09 paragraph 25: replaced the awkward phrase put away for themselves with keep ... to themselves while retaining the refusal to privatize ascent.
EP09 paragraph 31: after the cross-essay audit, changed the recalled word from compelled to forced, matching EP01 paragraphs 11 and 33.
EP10 paragraph 38: made the bedtime-story sentence idiomatic while preserving what neither the child nor the adult can identify.
unresolved: EP06 paragraph 56: the source’s pronoun 他 follows the parent example, while the ensuing counterquestion speaks from the Platonic condition. The English retains he rather than inserting an attribution absent from the source. This does not block the translation.

checks.source_markup_and_link_preservation: passed, tag sequences match paragraph by paragraph

findings: Restored all 64 source paragraphs, including the remuneration argument, the parent’s transition, the shared silence over the worst case, the two-level qualification, and the entire unanswered counterquestion.
Removed the abbreviated reconstruction’s added institutional remedies and claim that the final scene is an irony the dialogue never resolves.
Kept the benefit of the ruled as a constitutive condition of ruling, not merely the ruler’s benevolent intention; restored the separate question of who can verify its application.

Batch reread and the independent audit: changed disposal to handling in paragraph 50 to name a relation to a thing rather than imply discarding; kept reward broader than monetary payment in paragraph 18.
anchors: Paragraphs 22–26: both accounts change conceptual boundaries rather than offer unfavorable judgments.
Paragraphs 30–38: speaking and being heard do not substitute for a real stopping point; refusing medical consent is the concrete example.
Paragraphs 40–46: the craft’s public condition differs from a second position able to check its application.
Paragraphs 48–51: Plato’s lack of a name and SAE’s refusal to evaluate remain distinct shared limitations.
Paragraphs 53–59: not-given applies at one level; exchange and revocability below it remain explicit, and the practical transition is left unanswered.

findings: Restored all 47 source paragraphs, including the rule’s change from production to justice, the workplace and team examples, Adeimantus’ concrete objections, and the full standing-watch challenge.
Kept the city’s assignment distinct from the person’s establishment of their own law; accurate recognition remains a question on both sides.

Restored the source’s concessions to Plato: his care for individuals, the genuine attraction of shared care, and his explicit acknowledgment of the cost. No institutional solution was added to his counterquestion.

Batch reread: clarified the deck so that it unambiguously names the person as the one establishing their own law, and polished the English around one’s own and the statue without changing the argument.
anchors: Paragraphs 5–10: a rule governing productive work becomes a judgment governing people, and the harm is charged to the city.
Paragraphs 14–18: one’s own law is not a number adjusted by another; the opposed origins of one’s own are the point of comparison.
Paragraphs 24–36: the finger and statue images join the city’s good with the person’s good, without making Plato indifferent to the individual.
Paragraphs 39–42: lifelong necessary work and the ability to stop remain a practical unanswered challenge.
Paragraphs 44–47: shared care is genuinely attractive, but a finger cannot ask why it belongs to this hand.

findings: Restored all 56 source paragraphs, including each exchange in Socrates’ hesitation, the earth-birth story, the promotion/demotion clause, and the separate company and family examples.
Restored the explicit discipline of judging the move rather than convicting the storyteller and the distinct question of whether the story earned its warrant.
Removed the former added SAE response about domination and revisable solidarity; all three of Plato’s counterquestions remain open.
Batch reread: removed the narrowing word motives in paragraph 32 so the source’s separation of the move from good/bad evaluation remains general.
anchors: Paragraphs 1–22: gold first appears in selection by testing, and Socrates lays the fabrication before the reader rather than hiding it.
Paragraphs 27–31: moving gold from fire to blood changes whether the next question can be asked, not simply the story’s content.
Paragraphs 32–39: sincere motives and useful true stories do not alter the move; diagnosis is not a conviction of the storyteller.
Paragraphs 41–43: the nonhereditary mobility clause concentrates judgment in those claiming to discern invisible metal.
Paragraphs 48–52: fraternity, intergenerational transmission, and the unequal time needed to dismantle and build are three distinct unanswered objections.
Paragraphs 55–56: the maker’s explicit disbelief and preserved disclosure provide the first tool for later criticism.

findings: Restored all 60 source paragraphs, including the lead weights, Glaucon’s objection for absent people, all four grounds for return, the Chinese village example, and the full teaching scene.
Kept the four grounds distinct and preserved the different reasons SAE cannot take over each one; the fourth is explicitly independent of the preceding three.

Removed the abbreviated reconstruction’s added answers about specific obligations, contingent initiative, institution-building, and cultural reproduction. The origin of the first turn remains an unanswered question.

Batch reread and the independent audit: replaced cannot-not/cannot not in paragraphs 21, 22, and 28 with must/necessity. This is Plato’s ordinary necessity of return, not SAE’s technical 14DD cannot-not.
Cross-essay audit: paragraph 31 now recalls the word forced, matching EP01 paragraphs 11 and 33 rather than switching to compelled.
anchors: Paragraphs 13–22: whole-city benefit, debt of birth/nurture, superior ability, and unwillingness to rule are separate grounds.
Paragraphs 25–31: return is the second half of ascent, not charity or private property; the same compulsion word applies in both directions.
Paragraphs 34–36: later recognition can support the first compulsion but not the informed philosopher’s second descent.
Paragraphs 41–45: rejecting the premise of being made removes its debt, while ability alone supplies no duty.
Paragraphs 47–55: genuine teaching resists compulsion, and the first unreciprocated recognition is questioned without a supplied mechanism.
Paragraphs 58–60: temporary blindness, mockery, and the unreported duration and experience of adjustment remain in the ending.

findings: Restored all 61 source paragraphs, including the god’s single bed argument, Thales and Pythagoras, the measuring and visual examples, the comic mechanism, the poets’ insults, and the child’s repeated bedtime story.
Preserved both concessions to Plato: his admitted love of Homer and a verdict open to reversal through a prose defense of usefulness.
Removed the former invented SAE tests for distinguishing expression from manipulation. The same emotional gate, removal of the whole hand, and demand for a measure remain an unanswered challenge.

Batch reread: made the bedtime-story sentence in paragraph 38 idiomatic while retaining the child’s and adult’s inability to identify the relevant place; no interpretation of what it represents was added.
anchors: Paragraphs 7–16: the three beds, Homer’s practical accomplishments, user/maker/imitator, and appearance versus measurement remain distinct arguments.
Paragraphs 18–23: feeding grief and laughter loosens the same restraint used in one’s own affairs; dried out is explicitly Plato’s term.
Paragraphs 35–45: what the cut leaves outside remains, and poetry’s preserving it does not depend on solving or making it useful.
Paragraphs 47–48: Plato employs poetic craft and borrows Homer’s cadence without explaining the tension.
Paragraphs 50–55: expression and manipulation share a gate; no invented evaluative test resolves the defender’s own susceptibility.
Paragraphs 57–61: love, the severed remainder, the usefulness condition, and poetry’s nonreturn all remain in the ending.
